name: Hana Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a master’s degree, and I lead a team writing medical-equipment service software for a tech company. I know the code and delivery handoffs well, though I still ask the field desk about a strange case. Arman works as a physiotherapy assistant; with two school-age children, a mortgage and four months saved, I like getting a needed pump to the right clinic on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the medical-equipment service app still needs someone to notice when a replacement pump is sent to the wrong clinic. I use AI now and then to suggest a test, but I compare it with the service record before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m a team lead with a master’s degree and ordinary pay for this job. My husband Arman is a physiotherapy assistant; with two children, a mortgage and about four months saved, our work feels steady but a long illness would strain us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking equipment-service bookings and ask the field desk for two wrong-delivery cases each month. We’d keep putting 170 monthly into savings while both wages hold instead of replacing our working washing machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about this world. The machine at home is old, but we can keep it running and meet the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was a wrong delivery like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A portable pump was sent to a clinic across town while the waiting clinic needed it before opening. I traced the address from the service request to the van schedule and fixed the mismatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only occasional AI use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a colleague to show the tool catching a known error before I trust it on our schedule. A neat answer is not enough if the van still goes to the wrong door.

say: I tell coworkers **equipment deliveries** still need checks against service records.
I use **AI occasionally** after testing it on known errors.
think: I have **four months saved** on ordinary team-lead pay.
I see **two steady wages** covering our mortgage and children for now.
do: **Keep checking** service bookings and review two wrong deliveries monthly.
**Save 170 monthly** while both wages hold; keep the working washer.
feel: **Calm** about current work and household bills.
S0.quote: A neat answer is not enough if the van still goes to the wrong door.
fieldNote: She judges software by **real clinic deliveries**, not a clean screen.
Four months saved and **two wages** make the mild case secure, though illness could strain the budget.

steps.text: Keep checking equipment bookings and monthly wrong deliveries
Save 170 monthly while both household wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking booking, planning and coding will reach our service platform before a robot ever moves a pump. I would ask management which engineers still check delivery errors when a system writes the schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first-pass booking checks I oversee could disappear, leaving a smaller team to handle failures. My own hours could shrink even as Arman continues hands-on therapy work, and his wage alone would not cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn a new AI check for a pump sent to the wrong clinic, using fake clinic names and old service records after a colleague demonstrates it. In the first year I’d ask for a written team plan and check paid equipment-support openings if my hours fall; I would only move for pay covering our mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, although I can test a tool. I do not want fewer engineers blamed for the same wrong deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the portable-pump case and five other old address mistakes. If the AI sends one pump to the wrong site, I would keep a person on final dispatch checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Arman add more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He already works a full week and helps with the children. I would not build a plan around extra therapy hours that he has not been offered.

I want a **team plan** before first-pass booking work disappears.
think: I expect **routine booking checks** to shrink on my team.
I fear **my hours** could fall while Arman’s wage cannot carry the mortgage.
do: **Learn AI address checks** on fake clinics after a colleague demonstrates it.
**Request team plan** in the first year.
**Check paid equipment openings** if hours fall; move only for bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and accountability for delivery mistakes.
S1.quote: I do not want fewer engineers blamed for the same wrong deliveries.
fieldNote: She tests **AI dispatch checks** on six old address mistakes before trusting them.
Her **equipment-support search** depends on lost hours and a paid bill-covering offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could do nearly all the coding and service planning I lead. Robots that lift and deliver equipment might arrive around 2031, but my screen work faces the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the lead role could end before I find another software job, even though some firms are nearby. Four months saved and Arman’s wage give us time, but the mortgage and two children keep taking money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the old washer and ask the company for a written date if lead roles change. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d apply for paid equipment-service coordination only where vacancies exist and the wage covers our bills; I’d ask the lender about a payment plan before arrears if the search lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed. My family cannot live on a calendar full of possible interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them I am looking for work and their school routine will stay as steady as we can make it. I would not promise a new job until an employer signs the offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would equipment service stay human?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know; AGI could plan visits and robots later carry equipment. I would treat a paid coordination role as a bridge, not a lifetime shelter.

say: I say **thinking AGI by 2028** reaches my code and service planning.
I know **delivery robots around 2031** arrive later than my desk-work risk.
think: I expect my **lead role** could end despite nearby firms.
I know **four months saved** and Arman’s wage buy time, not permanence.
do: **Keep the old washer** and request a written lead-job date now.
**Apply for paid coordination** if displaced after 2028 and vacancies cover bills.
**Ask the lender** about payment terms before arrears if the search lasts.
feel: **Alarmed** by wage loss despite a four-month cushion.
S2.quote: My family cannot live on a calendar full of possible interviews.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 software date** from delivery robots around 2031.
The **lender question** is a hardship measure if the job search threatens arrears, with no income assumed from the bank.

steps.text: Keep the working washer instead of buying a replacement
Apply for paid equipment-coordination vacancies if displaced after 2028 and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives us time to learn why equipment is late, not only write a faster schedule. Robots for hands-on delivery may follow around 2034, so my coding changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better at talking through service failures with clinics, though AGI may handle those calls too. Arman and I could build a larger buffer if both wages continue and the washer survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the field-service manager for one anonymized late-delivery case each month to work through with her on paid time, and do it only if my own manager agrees too. We’d save 190 monthly if both wages hold; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d seek paid service-coordination roles only where vacancies remain and pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but able to prepare. A real late-delivery case would tell me more than a glossy course description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write on the case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic’s request, the van assignment and the time the pump actually arrived. I would ask the service manager where my explanation missed a handoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if either manager refuses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my lead job and ask for old reports with clinic names removed during normal paid work, if approved. I would not pretend a declined visit had trained me.

say: I want **late deliveries** studied before AGI reaches service code in 2031.
I know **delivery robots around 2034** may follow later.
think: I might learn **clinic service problems**, though AGI could handle calls too.
I could build **more savings** if both wages continue.
do: **Study monthly delivery cases** with both managers’ paid-time approval; otherwise use anonymized reports with my manager’s paid-time approval.
**Seek paid service coordination** if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover mortgage.
feel: **Anxious but prepared** if approved real cases are available.
S3.quote: A real late-delivery case would tell me more than a glossy course description.
fieldNote: Her **case learning** requires two managers and paid time before she gains service experience.
The **saving plan** remains independent of training and requires both wages.

steps.text: Study monthly anonymized delivery cases only with both managers approving paid time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets us improve the household buffer and make equipment service records clearer. Robots for hands-on delivery may follow around 2039, after the code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but I cannot assume they pay our mortgage. I might build six months of bills if both jobs continue, yet even service planning could be automated by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the service platform and record one solved delivery error monthly without clinic names. We would pay 120 extra toward mortgage principal while both wages hold; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid service-quality work only where vacancies remain and the pay covers our bills. We would move only after a written paid offer covers bills, new housing, school travel and moving costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the eventual change, but secure in the next few years. I like knowing exactly what we can save before promising the children anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The original service request, the mistaken route and what we changed before the pump arrived. I could show how I fixed a late delivery without showing a clinic’s details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for service work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer covering bills, new housing, school travel and moving costs. We have some local developer options, so I would test them first.

I could build **six months of bills** if both jobs continue.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my service-planning code and lead role could end before a paid alternative is clear. A written job date and a real equipment-coordination opening that covers our bills would help while we use the four-month buffer carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who has to explain a missing pump to the clinic. A missing clinic pump needs a named person who can trace the request before the next patient arrives.

headlineQuote: A missing clinic pump needs a named person who can trace the request before the next patient arrives.
portrait: Hana is a **43-year-old team lead** with a master’s degree, typical pay and four months of expenses saved.
She and Arman support **two children** and a mortgage, with his physiotherapy work mostly hands-on.
She uses AI **occasionally after proof**, checking schedules against actual clinic service records.
Her **2028 worry** is losing the lead wage before paid service work is clear; delivery robots follow later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead wage while the household still has a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date**, bill-covering paid equipment-coordination opening and careful use of savings would help.
